About fifty years, from 235 to 284, when the Roman Empire nearly fell apart under civil wars, invasions, plague and failing money. It began when soldiers killed the emperor Severus Alexander in 235 and ended when Diocletian took power in 284.

  • More than twenty emperors ruled, most of them generals raised by their troops, and most died by violence.
  • Goths and other peoples raided across the Rhine and Danube; one army killed the emperor Decius in 251.
  • In the east, the Sasanian king Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian in 260.
  • The Plague of Cyprian cut the population, and the silver coinage collapsed.

For about fourteen years the empire split into three: the Gallic Empire in the west, the Palmyrene state of Zenobia in the east, and Rome in between. Aurelian put it back together by 274 and gave Rome new walls. The reforms that followed made a different, more military state, and historians use the crisis to mark the start of late antiquity.
